choices: False — feasible only means it satisfies the constraints
checkpoints.explanation: Feasible just means all constraints hold. Optimal is the stronger property: feasible and no feasible point has better cost. Keeping these separate is essential vocabulary.
checkpoints.question: True or false: a feasible solution must minimize the objective function.

choices: A guarantee that the optimal solution is unique
checkpoints.explanation: A mathematical program supplies variables, an objective, and constraints — but nothing promises the optimum is unique or even exists. Ties and unbounded problems are both possible.
checkpoints.question: Every mathematical program has three ingredients. Which of these is NOT one of them?

choices: Always equal to the integer program's optimal value
At least as good — an optimistic bound on it
Unrelated to the integer program's value
checkpoints.explanation: Relaxing constraints can only enlarge the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum is at least as good as the original's — an optimistic bound. It may be fractional and strictly better.
checkpoints.question: Take an integer program and relax (drop) the integrality requirement. The optimal value of the resulting LP is…

checkpoints.explanation: You cannot buy 3.7 trucks. The decision is inherently whole-numbered, which breaks divisibility and turns the model into an integer program.
checkpoints.question: Your model has a variable x = number of delivery trucks to purchase. Which LP axiom is at risk?

choices: The number of units of product A to make
The $40 profit per unit of A
checkpoints.explanation: The 200 hours, the $40 profit, and the constraint count are fixed data. Decision variables are the quantities of products to make.
checkpoints.question: In the production-planning LP, which of these is a decision variable?

choices: The 5-consecutive-days rule can't be captured with y_j
y_j would have to be fractional
checkpoints.explanation: With y_j = nurses working day j, there is no way to write 'each nurse works 5 consecutive days' linearly. Choosing x_j = nurses starting on day j bakes the rule into the model. Variable choice is a design decision!
checkpoints.question: In the nurse-scheduling model, why did we use x_j = nurses starting their week on day j, instead of y_j = nurses working on day j?

checkpoints.explanation: Whole trucks are a discrete decision, so this is a mixed-integer program. Dropping the whole-number requirement produces its LP relaxation.
checkpoints.question: A city must buy delivery trucks — whole trucks only — to serve routes at minimum cost. Which flavor of optimization is that?

checkpoints.explanation: An equality is exactly the intersection of the two opposing inequalities: a'x = b if and only if a'x ≥ b and a'x ≤ b.
checkpoints.question: An equality constraint a'x = b can be replaced by…

choices: If n² is odd, then n is odd
If n² is even, then n is even
If n is even, then n² is even
If n² is odd, then n is even
checkpoints.explanation: For P ⇒ Q with P = 'n odd', Q = 'n² odd': the contrapositive is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, i.e. 'if n² is even, then n is even'.
checkpoints.question: Claim: if n is odd, then n² is odd. Which statement is its contrapositive?

choices: It is false for some larger n
Induction now finishes the proof automatically
checkpoints.explanation: A million confirmations are evidence, not proof — remember n² + n + 41 surviving 39 checks. Until there's a proof, the honest status is 'open'.
checkpoints.question: A conjecture has been verified by computer for n = 1 up to 10⁶. What do we know?

checkpoints.explanation: There's nothing to construct — you rule the object out. Assume a smallest positive rational q exists; then q/2 is a smaller one. Contradiction.
checkpoints.question: Which technique fits best: “there is no smallest positive rational number”?

lectures.description: Logical implication, proof techniques, counterexamples, mathematical writing, and a practical introduction to LaTeX.
lectures.title: Proof Techniques & LaTeX

choices: The intersection of two convex sets
checkpoints.explanation: A star has 'dents': pick two points on different arms and the segment leaves the set. Halfspaces, segments, and intersections of convex sets are always convex — that last fact is exactly why polyhedra are convex.
checkpoints.question: Which of these sets is NOT convex?

choices: Show every pair y, z ∈ P has x between them
Exhibit some y, z ∈ P ∖ {x} and λ ∈ [0, 1] with x = λy + (1 − λ)z
Show x is not optimal for any cost vector
Show fewer than n constraints exist
checkpoints.explanation: Not extreme means the definition fails: there EXIST y, z in P (both ≠ x) with x on the segment between them — you must exhibit them. Getting the negation right is half the proof.
checkpoints.question: To prove x ∈ P is not an extreme point, you must…

checkpoints.explanation: The bound is (m choose n): a basic solution needs n linearly independent active constraints chosen from the m available, and each such choice pins down at most one point.
checkpoints.question: With m constraints in ℝⁿ, the number of basic solutions is at most…

lectures.description: Convexity, polyhedra, extreme points, vertices, basic feasible solutions, and adjacency.
lectures.title: The Geometry of Linear Programming I

checkpoints.explanation: In standard form, nonbasic variables (n − m of them) are zero by construction. Degeneracy means MORE than n − m zeros — some basic variable is zero too. Here n − m = 7 − 4 = 3.
checkpoints.question: Standard form, n = 7 variables, m = 4 equations. A basic solution is degenerate when…

checkpoints.explanation: A halfplane contains lines, so it has no extreme point (Thm 2.6). The square and triangle are polytopes; standard-form polyhedra always have a BFS by Corollary 2.2.
checkpoints.question: Which polyhedron has no extreme point?

choices: Every optimal solution is an extreme point
At least one optimal solution is an extreme point
checkpoints.explanation: Thm 2.7 says SOME optimal solution is at an extreme point — others may exist (a whole optimal edge, say). It does not force uniqueness or boundedness.
checkpoints.question: P has an extreme point and the LP has an optimal solution. Which is guaranteed?

lectures.description: Standard-form bases, degeneracy, existence and optimality of extreme points, convex hulls, and Fourier–Motzkin elimination.
lectures.title: The Geometry of Linear Programming II

checkpoints.explanation: A pivot changes the basis, dictionary, and usually the current endpoint. It does not change the feasible polyhedron defined by the original constraints.
checkpoints.question: What remains unchanged during a simplex pivot?

choices: The current basic feasible solution is optimal
The current basic feasible solution is unique
checkpoints.explanation: Primal feasibility and nonnegative nonbasic reduced costs are the two checks for an optimal basis. They do not imply uniqueness or boundedness.
checkpoints.question: For a feasible basis in a minimization LP, what does every nonbasic reduced cost being nonnegative certify?

choices: The ratio test chooses the largest component of u
The direction is blocked at step zero
The path stays feasible for every nonnegative step and the objective is unbounded below
checkpoints.explanation: When u ≤ 0, the basic part of the direction is −u ≥ 0, so no variable blocks the improving move. The resulting feasible ray certifies unboundedness below.
checkpoints.question: An entering variable has negative reduced cost and u = B⁻¹Aⱼ ≤ 0. What follows?

choices: The entering variable has zero reduced cost
x₆ remains basic at value zero because two ratio-test rows tied
checkpoints.explanation: The ratio test tied in the x₅ and x₆ rows. After x₅ leaves, x₆ remains in the basis at value zero, which is exactly degeneracy.
checkpoints.question: Why is x⁽¹⁾ = (10, 0, 0, 10, 0, 0) degenerate after x₁ enters and x₅ leaves?

lectures.description: Basis partitions, equality-preserving feasible directions, maximum feasible steps, reduced costs, and the basis optimality test.
lectures.title: Simplex I: Basis Directions and Reduced Costs

choices: Yes — adjacent bases always represent adjacent vertices
No — several bases can represent the same point, so the step can have length zero
Yes, provided the entering reduced cost is negative
No — a degenerate basis can never pivot
checkpoints.explanation: Simplex moves between bases. At a degenerate BFS, a one-column exchange can change the basis while leaving both the feasible point and objective value unchanged.
checkpoints.question: At a degenerate basic feasible solution, does exchanging one basis column always move to a distinct vertex?

choices: Every row, using the absolute value of uᵢ
Only rows whose basic value is strictly positive
checkpoints.explanation: When uᵢ > 0, the component x_B,i − θuᵢ decreases and can hit zero. Rows with uᵢ ≤ 0 do not impose an upper bound on a nonnegative step.
checkpoints.question: For u = B⁻¹Aⱼ, which rows constrain the positive step θ in x_B(θ) = x_B − θu?

choices: An improving objective slope, but not necessarily a positive step
That the current point is not optimal
checkpoints.explanation: A negative reduced cost prices the basic direction: its objective slope is negative. A zero basic component can still block that direction at θ = 0.
checkpoints.question: At a degenerate BFS in a minimization problem, what does c̄ⱼ < 0 guarantee?

choices: B⁻¹b ≥ 0 and every nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative
B⁻¹b = 0 and every nonbasic reduced cost is negative
B is nonsingular and the objective value is negative
Every basic variable and every reduced cost is strictly positive
checkpoints.explanation: B⁻¹b ≥ 0 supplies primal feasibility. Nonnegative nonbasic reduced costs show that no feasible nonbasic displacement can lower the objective.
checkpoints.question: Which pair certifies that a basis is optimal for this minimization LP?
